summary_html: CPS **screens out** a report (no investigation) or closes as **unfounded** after minimal review. Federal law (CAPTA) conditions funding on operating screening criteria and recordkeeping; federal reviews (CFSR) assess decision quality.
authority_html:
- **CAPTA (42 U.S.C. §§ 5101–5116)** — screening & intake system requirements  
- **CFSR Regulations (45 CFR Part 1355)** — federal performance/quality review of state screening and responses

primary_citations.citation_text: Texas - Texas Family Code Chapter 261 (Investigation of Report of Child Abuse or Neglect)
Texas - Texas Family Code Chapter 262 (Procedures in Suit by Governmental Entity to Protect Health and Safety of Child)

case_law.method: v1.1.0 case-law rebuild: authorities selected per decision point, each opinion retrieved from CourtListener and read; holding and quote taken from the opinion text; independently re-verified before release. Previous keyword-matched Justia listings were removed.

key_cases.holding: Texas does not recognize a negligence per se claim for failing to report child abuse under Family Code § 261.109; the reporting duty is enforced criminally, not through private tort liability.
key_cases.relevance: The controlling Texas answer to the question families ask at this node: the § 261.101 duty to report and the § 261.109 misdemeanor for failing to report create no private cause of action, so a failure to report (or to act on a report) is punished criminally and administratively, not in a civil damages suit.
key_cases.quote: we hold that it is not appropriate to adopt Family Code section 261.109(a) as establishing a duty and standard of conduct in tort

key_cases.case_name: DeShaney v. Winnebago County Department of Social Services
key_cases.court: Supreme Court of the United States
key_cases.holding: The Due Process Clause imposes no general affirmative duty on a child-protection agency to protect a child from private violence, even where the agency knew of the danger and failed to act.
key_cases.relevance: Marks the constitutional boundary at this node: outside state custody there is no affirmative federal duty to protect, so a failure here is answerable through state law, licensing and federal funding conditions rather than § 1983 — which is why the Texas remedy has been systemic litigation (M.D. v. Abbott) rather than individual damages.
key_cases.quote: a State's failure to protect an individual against private violence simply does not constitute a violation of the Due Process Clause

search_keywords: Texas Department of Family and Protective Services

state_agency.name: Texas Department of Family and Protective Services

notice_requirements.timing: In writing before the department conducts an interview with an alleged perpetrator; the person signs the written notice to acknowledge receipt (Tex. Fam. Code § 261.3091(a))
content_required: That the person may request an administrative review of the department's findings under Tex. Fam. Code § 261.309 (Tex. Fam. Code § 261.3091(a))

Administrative review of a disputed determination of whether child abuse or neglect occurred is conducted by a department employee in administration who was not involved in and did not directly supervise the investigation, and the review must sustain, alter, or reverse the department's original findings (Tex. Fam. Code § 261.309(c))

The review must be conducted as soon as possible but not later than the 45th day after the date the department receives the request, unless the department has good cause for extending the deadline or a related court proceeding or criminal investigation is pending (Tex. Fam. Code § 261.309(d))
notice_requirements.defective_notice_consequence: Not specified in Tex. Fam. Code § 261.3091; the department must document in the case file that it provided the notice (Tex. Fam. Code § 261.3091(b)). A person is not required to exhaust the review remedy before pursuing a judicial remedy provided by law (Tex. Fam. Code § 261.309(e)), and when a finding is overturned the department must remove the person's name from the central registry not later than the 10th business day after it receives notice (Tex. Fam. Code § 261.002(b)(3))
